title: ICMR Standard Treatment Guidelines: Clinical Management of Dengue in India
license: Government of India Open Access / Public Health Guidance

sections.title: Epidemiology in Indian Context and Diagnosis
sections.content: In India, dengue is hyperendemic across urban, semi-urban, and rural districts with peak incidence during the post-monsoon months. Laboratory confirmation: NS1 antigen ELISA is recommended during days 1 to 5 of fever; IgM antibody ELISA is recommended from day 5 onwards. A complete blood count (CBC) with hematocrit and platelet count must be performed at baseline and monitored regularly during the transition to the critical phase.

sections.title: Platelet Count Thresholds and Transfusion Warnings
sections.content: A common clinical misconception in India is the premature transfusion of platelets based solely on low platelet numbers. ICMR guidelines explicitly recommend against prophylactic platelet transfusions when the platelet count is >20,000/μL in the absence of significant clinical bleeding. Prophylactic transfusion does not prevent severe bleeding, does not hasten recovery, carries risks of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and fluid overload, and exhausts blood bank supplies. Platelet transfusion is indicated primarily when platelet count is <10,000/μL or in the presence of active, systemic mucosal or internal bleeding.

sections.title: Fluid Therapy and Hematocrit Monitoring
sections.content: The cornerstone of dengue management is tailored fluid therapy. Hematocrit serves as an objective surrogate for plasma leakage. A rising hematocrit (>20% increase from baseline) indicates significant plasma leakage and hemoconcentration, necessitating prompt isotonic crystalloid replacement (Normal Saline 0.9% or Ringer's Lactate). Overzealous fluid administration must be avoided during the recovery phase to prevent pulmonary edema.

sections.title: Danger Signs and Immediate Referral Criteria
sections.content: Patients exhibiting any of the following must be immediately escalated to emergency secondary/tertiary facilities: cold, clammy extremities with feeble rapid pulse (dengue shock syndrome), postural hypotension, oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h), sudden drop in temperature with clinical deterioration, persistent vomiting, or coffee-ground hematemesis/melena.

title: ICMR Guidelines for Management of Type 2 Diabetes in South Asian Phenotypes
license: Government of India Open Access / Public Health Guidance

sections.title: The South Asian Diabetes Phenotype and Diagnostic Criteria
sections.content: Indians and South Asians have a unique phenotype ('Asian Indian Phenotype') characterized by high body fat percentage, increased visceral adiposity, higher insulin resistance, and lower skeletal muscle mass despite a normal or lower Body Mass Index (BMI). Screening should begin at age 30 or earlier in the presence of risk factors. Diagnosis: Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), 2-hour post-load glucose during 75g OGTT ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), or HbA1c ≥6.5%.

sections.title: Glycemic Targets and Pharmacotherapy
sections.content: The general glycemic target for non-pregnant adults with type 2 diabetes is HbA1c <7.0%, fasting glucose 80-130 mg/dL, and postprandial glucose <180 mg/dL. First-line pharmacotherapy in the absence of contraindications is Metformin, initiated with lifestyle intervention. In individuals with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists with proven benefit are recommended as part of the regimen.

sections.title: Dietary Principles and Physical Activity for Indian Diets
sections.content: Traditional Indian diets frequently derive >65-75% of calories from carbohydrates, predominantly refined grains (white rice, refined wheat flour). ICMR recommends reducing carbohydrate intake to 50-55% of total daily energy, increasing protein to 15-20% (through legumes, pulses, paneer, eggs, soy), and incorporating high dietary fiber (>30-40 g/day). Sedentary lifestyle must be counteracted with at least 150 minutes per week of brisk walking or moderate physical activity.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia Emergency Recognition and Management
sections.content: Hypoglycemia (blood glucose <70 mg/dL) is an acute clinical risk, especially with sulfonylureas and insulin. Symptoms include trembling, diaphoresis, palpitations, anxiety, hunger, dizziness, and cognitive confusion. Immediate treatment is the 'Rule of 15': ingest 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate (3-4 glucose tablets, half glass of fruit juice, or 3 teaspoons of sugar dissolved in water), recheck blood glucose after 15 minutes, and repeat if still <70 mg/dL.

title: ICMR Clinical Guidelines for Acute Respiratory Infections and Pneumonia
license: Government of India Open Access / Public Health Guidance

sections.title: Clinical Stratification of Upper vs Lower Respiratory Infections
sections.content: Acute Upper Respiratory Infections (URI), including the common cold, viral pharyngitis, and rhinovirus infection, present with nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, mild sore throat, and low-grade fever. Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) like pneumonia involve alveolar consolidation. Respiratory rate (tachypnea) is the single most sensitive physical examination sign for pneumonia: age >5 years / adults: >20 breaths/min; children 1-5 years: >40 breaths/min; infants 2-11 months: >50 breaths/min.

sections.title: Red-Flag Symptoms Requiring Emergency Care
sections.content: Immediate emergency evaluation is indicated when any of the following signs appear: severe shortness of breath or inability to complete a full sentence without gasping; pulse oximetry SpO2 <93% on room air; cyanosis of lips or nail beds; stridor or grunting; chest indrawing; hemoptysis; confusion or lethargy; or new onset systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg (septic shock warning).
